Positioning: Choosing the Comparison in Which You Win

Two operators, a hardware-plus-software company in Coimbatore and an AI-native legal product in Pune, are each about to make the same decision in different clothes: which set of alternatives their buyer should have in mind at the moment of judgement. Everything downstream — price, buying committee, roadmap, sales cost, even the multiple an acquirer will pay — follows from that choice.

1. Two Decisions, Six Weeks Apart

On 14 August 2025, Devika Raghunathan sat in the mezzanine meeting room above Samarth Instruments' test floor in Coimbatore, with two documents in front of her that disagreed. The first was a quotation comparison forwarded by a procurement manager at a large electric three-wheeler fleet in Indore. It placed Samarth's SX-40 battery diagnostic system — a clamp-on impedance spectroscopy unit with a thermal probe and a cloud analytics service that estimates pack state-of-health — in a table alongside two imported benchtop testers and one Chinese portable unit. Four columns: measurement channels, frequency range, IP rating, price. Samarth was third on price and second on channels. The procurement manager had written, in the body of the email, a single line: "Please advise best commercial for equivalent spec."

The second document was a one-page memo from a non-banking finance company in Ahmedabad that funds electric three-wheelers for last-mile delivery operators. The NBFC had been receiving Samarth's state-of-health reports as a courtesy, because one of its borrowers happened to be a Samarth customer. Its credit team had used eleven months of those reports to re-estimate the residual value of repossessed vehicles, and had concluded that packs they had been writing down to ₹0 at thirty months were, in about four cases out of ten, worth ₹38,000 to ₹52,000 in the second-life market. The memo asked whether Samarth could supply such reports for the NBFC's whole book of 14,200 vehicles, and what that would cost.

Samarth had shipped 3,100 units at an average selling price of ₹4.2 lakh, closing FY25 at ₹96 crore of revenue and a blended gross margin of 38 per cent, which had fallen four points in two years. Devika had forty field engineers, a plant in Chennai, and a Series C of about ₹120 crore that her chief executive wanted to raise in the first quarter of the coming financial year. Her problem was not that she had no answer to the procurement manager. It was that answering him at all conceded a frame of reference in which Samarth's most valuable property — eleven months of longitudinal pack data and a residual-value model nobody else in India had — did not appear as a column.

Six weeks later and 1,200 kilometres north-west, on 9 September 2025, Anirudh Bose was having a version of the same argument with his own sales leader in a rented floor in Baner, Pune. Saumitra Legal Intelligence sold an AI-native contract review system: it ingested vendor and customer contracts, extracted obligations and renewal dates, and flagged deviations from a client's negotiation playbook. Thirty-four customers, ₹21 crore of annual recurring revenue, an average contract value of ₹62 lakh, and gross margin of 71 per cent after inference costs. The sales leader wanted to keep selling against contract lifecycle management suites, where the buyer was a general counsel's operations lead, the budget line was legal technology, the unit was a seat at ₹8,000 to ₹12,000 a month, and the evaluation was a feature checklist Saumitra kept losing on — clause library depth, e-signature integration, workflow builder.

Anirudh wanted to sell against the legal process outsourcing vendor. One prospect, a listed auto-components manufacturer, was paying an LPO roughly ₹1,800 per contract reviewed across about 40,000 contracts a year: ₹7.2 crore, sitting in professional services, owned not by the general counsel's ops lead but by the chief financial officer, and subject to an annual cost-reduction target. In that frame Saumitra had no clause library to be scored on. It had a single question to answer — could it do the review at human-comparable quality — and a price ceiling set by ₹7.2 crore rather than by seat counts. It also had an indemnity conversation nobody at Saumitra wanted to have, and a quality bar that a checklist-based frame would never have imposed.

Saumitra's price list was being reissued on 1 November. Samarth's board met in the last week of September. Both decisions were, at bottom, the same decision, and it is the decision this page is about.

2. The Idea, Stated Precisely

Positioning is the deliberate choice of the comparison set in which a product will be evaluated, together with the claim about which dimension of that comparison is decisive. It has two components and practitioners routinely attend to only the second. The first component is the frame of reference: the set of alternatives — including doing nothing, doing it manually, and doing it with staff — that the buyer holds in mind at the moment of judgement. The second is the point of difference: the attribute on which you claim superiority within that set, and which the buyer can verify at acceptable cost. A product's commercial fate is usually determined more by the first than the second, which is counter-intuitive, because the second is what marketing departments spend their time writing.

The formal ancestor of the idea is older than marketing as a discipline. Harold Hotelling's 1929 model of two ice-cream vendors on a beach gave economics the vocabulary of location in an attribute space and the result that competitors converge toward the centre. Kelvin Lancaster's 1966 reformulation of consumer theory — that buyers derive utility not from goods but from the characteristics goods contain — supplied the coordinate system. Wendell Smith had already, in 1956, drawn the distinction that still causes confusion in product meetings: product differentiation bends demand toward a supply-side choice, while market segmentation adapts supply to heterogeneous demand. Theodore Levitt's "Marketing Myopia" of 1960 was, read carefully, a paper about frames of reference: his railroads failed not because they were badly run but because they had adopted a comparison set ("other railroads") that excluded the alternatives their customers were actually choosing.

The word itself arrived through practice. Al Ries and Jack Trout published a series in Industrial Marketing in 1969 and a book in 1981, arguing that in a communications-saturated environment the scarce resource is not attention but an unoccupied slot in a prospect's memory. The problem positioning was invented to solve was therefore not "how do we describe our product" but "given that the buyer already has a mental filing system, which drawer do we get filed in, and what is already in that drawer". Academic marketing built the measurement apparatus in parallel: Green and Rao's multidimensional scaling in 1972 turned similarity judgements into perceptual maps; Green and Srinivasan's 1978 survey of conjoint analysis made attribute trade-offs estimable; McFadden's 1974 conditional logit made market share a computable function of a choice set. Geoffrey Moore's 1991 template — for [target], who [need], our [product] is a [category] that [benefit]; unlike [alternative], we [differentiator] — compressed all of it into a sentence, and by doing so obscured that the hard work is in the two bracketed terms, category and alternative, not in the benefit clause everyone rewrites.

April Dunford's 2019 reformulation is the version most product organisations now use, and its contribution is procedural rather than theoretical: it insists you derive the category last, from competitive alternatives, unique attributes, value and best-fit customers, instead of choosing a fashionable category first and reverse-engineering a story into it. The companion page to this one works through that derivation. What follows assumes it and pushes past it, because the derivation has a hole in the middle: it tells you how to find a defensible frame, not how to choose between two defensible frames that lead to different companies. That is what Devika and Anirudh are each facing.

The schools, and the propositions each will and will not sign

Positioning is unusual among product-management topics in that the disagreement about it is real, well-evidenced on multiple sides, and load-bearing. It is worth being precise about who holds what, because a senior practitioner is often refereeing an argument in which two competent people are each applying a coherent school without naming it.

3. Mechanics: What Experts Actually Do, Including the Steps Left Implicit

The published procedures list competitive alternatives, unique attributes, value, best-fit customers and category. Watching senior practitioners do the work, three steps appear that none of the procedures name, and they are where the difficulty lives.

The first implicit step is sourcing the alternatives from transaction evidence rather than from a competitive matrix. A competitive matrix is built by product marketing from the vendors it fears. The real alternative set lives in closed-lost reasons, in the first two minutes of discovery calls, and in the sentence buyers use when they describe what they do today. Devika's team ran this exercise over sixty deals from the previous four quarters and coded the "what will you do if you do not buy" field. Twenty-two deals named an imported tester. Nine named a Chinese portable unit. Twenty-nine named something that was not an instrument at all: a service contract with the pack supplier, a rule of thumb ("we replace at thirty months"), or nothing. Almost half of Samarth's competitive reality was outside the frame in which its own datasheet was written. That ratio — between forty and sixty per cent non-product alternatives — recurs often enough across categories that its absence is itself a diagnostic: if your closed-lost data shows only named vendors, your sales team is filling the field from a picklist, not from the buyer.

The second implicit step is identifying the ledger. Every frame of reference implies a budget line, an owner of that line, and a set of other things competing for it. This is the step that converts positioning from a communications exercise into a commercial one. Selling Samarth as an instrument means drawing on a capital equipment budget, owned by a plant or maintenance head, approved against a depreciation schedule, and competing with a welding rig. Selling it as residual-value assurance means drawing on a credit-risk or provisioning line, owned by a chief risk officer, approved against expected loss, and competing with nothing much, because the line has no other vendors on it. The same box of electronics. Two different companies.

The third implicit step is checking that the frame is cheap for the buyer to verify. A frame in which your advantage is real but expensive to confirm converts your differentiation into the buyer's cost, and buyers charge you for it in cycle time. This is the most common reason a technically correct reframe underperforms in the field.

The formal treatment, worked

Two pieces of quantitative machinery are worth carrying, because they make explicit what positioning arguments usually leave to taste.

The first is economic value to the customer, which says that the ceiling on what a rational buyer will pay is the price of their next-best alternative, plus the monetised value of what you do better, minus the monetised value of what you do worse. The important word is alternative: EVC is not computable until the frame is fixed. Change the frame and you change every term. Anirudh's team ran the arithmetic across three candidate frames for the auto-components prospect in September.

The second piece of machinery is the discrete-choice model, which formalises what positioning does in a way most practitioners never see stated. In a conditional logit, the probability that a buyer chooses option i from a set S is exp(Vi) divided by the sum of exp(Vj) over all j in S, where V is deterministic utility. Positioning acts on this expression in two distinct ways. Differentiation raises your own Vi. Framing changes which alternatives appear in S at all. The second lever is almost always larger, and this is the mathematical statement of why reframing outperforms message-polishing.

Take Samarth's numbers. Suppose in Frame A the buyer's utility is driven by measurement channels, price and brand familiarity, and that on that scale the two imported testers score V = 1.4 and 1.2, the Chinese portable scores 0.9, and Samarth scores 1.3. Exponentiating and normalising gives Samarth 4.06 / (4.06 + 3.32 + 2.46 + 3.67) = about 30 per cent — close to the 31 per cent win rate observed. Now improve Samarth's product until its utility rises from 1.3 to 1.6, a genuinely expensive engineering programme. Share rises to about 36 per cent. Six points for a year of work. Now instead change the set: in Frame B, the alternatives are "manual write-down rule" at V = 0.3 and "do nothing" at V = 0.1, and Samarth's utility, scored on the criteria that frame makes salient, is 1.5. Share becomes 4.48 / (4.48 + 1.35 + 1.11) = about 65 per cent. The observed 62 per cent in the paired deals is within noise of that. The engineering programme bought six points; the reframe bought thirty-four.

The model carries a caveat worth knowing, because it generates practical advice. Logit assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives: the ratio of any two options' probabilities is unaffected by what else is in the set. That assumption fails precisely when alternatives are near-substitutes, which is the normal case in a crowded frame. A nested formulation, in which near-identical options compete within a nest before nests compete with each other, is more realistic and has a blunt implication: adding a lookalike competitor to a crowded frame takes share disproportionately from the option it most resembles — which is you. Sitting in a frame where three vendors look like you is materially worse than the naive arithmetic suggests. This is the formal shadow of the practitioner's instinct that "we keep getting compared to the wrong people".

Second-order effects, which is where the money is

Frames propagate. The most consequential propagations are invisible for two or three quarters and then become structural.

The frame sets the roadmap rubric. If you compete in Frame A, your win-loss reports will tell you you lost on channel count and IP rating, and a disciplined product team will dutifully close those gaps. Eighteen months later you have a product optimised against a rival's datasheet, built by engineers whose intuitions have been trained on someone else's criteria. Devika could point at three features in the SX-40 that existed solely because a competitor's brochure listed them, consuming an estimated eleven engineer-months, used by fewer than four per cent of customers.

The frame sets the hiring profile, and hiring is stickier than messaging. A company selling instruments hires application engineers who can talk about frequency sweeps. A company selling risk assurance hires people who can sit with a chief risk officer and discuss expected loss. You can rewrite a website in a fortnight. Rebuilding a twenty-person commercial team around a different conversation takes a year and costs most of the existing team.

The frame determines who values you, and at what. This is the effect boards understand and product teams often do not. Comparable-company multiples are assigned by category. An instrument manufacturer in India trades against other instrument manufacturers; a risk-data business trades against data businesses. The spread between those comparable sets, in Devika's own banker's framing, was two-to-three times revenue against six-to-nine. On ₹96 crore of revenue that is a difference of several hundred crore of enterprise value attributable to nothing but the frame — which is why positioning decisions that look like marketing decisions get made in board meetings.

The frame determines whether demand already exists. Selling into an established frame means inheriting existing search behaviour, existing analyst taxonomies, existing procurement categories and existing budget lines. Selling into a new frame means creating all four at your own expense. Category creation is not a positioning choice with a communications cost; it is a demand-generation liability carried on the balance sheet of the marketing plan, and it should be underwritten like one.

4. Conditions, Stated as Testable Claims

Whether positioning is the right lever is an empirical question with checkable conditions. Five are worth stating as claims that can be falsified with data a competent team already has.

C1: Buyers face a live comparison. Test: in the last fifty closed-lost records, at least sixty per cent name a specific alternative. If most say "no decision" or "budget", the problem is demand, not frame. Devika: passes — fifty-one of sixty named something. Anirudh: passes, but the alternative named differs by frame, which is itself the finding.

C2: The difference is verifiable inside the buyer's evaluation budget. Test: can a sceptical buyer confirm your claim in one working session with data they already hold? Devika: fails in Frame B without help — residual-value accuracy takes months of pack history to prove, which is why she later constructs a retrospective test on the NBFC's own repossessed vehicles. Anirudh: passes in Frame 3 by running a blind benchmark on five hundred already-reviewed contracts, an afternoon of the client's time.

C3: The strength is unequally distributed. Test: would a competitor's own sales engineer concede it in private? Devika: passes — no rival has eleven months of Indian three-wheeler pack telemetry. Anirudh: partially fails; extraction accuracy is a moving target that a well-funded rival can match in two quarters, which pushes him toward claims grounded in playbook customisation and audit trail rather than raw model quality.

C4: There is a segment with a steep value gradient. Test: does willingness-to-pay vary by more than three times across identified segments for the same functionality? If it is flat, you have a commodity and should optimise distribution. Devika: passes emphatically — a fleet operator values the SX-40 at its equipment price; an NBFC values the same output at a multiple of it.

C5: You can fund what the frame requires. Test: does the frame demand demand-creation, evidence, or obligations you cannot presently afford? Anirudh: the outsourcing frame demands an accuracy commitment with financial consequence; Saumitra's insurance and balance sheet must support it, or the frame is aspirational.

There are also conditions under which the idea is actively misleading, and a senior practitioner should be able to name them without embarrassment. In mature, low-involvement categories where products genuinely are similar and buying is habitual, the empirical-generalisation school is probably right: effort spent sharpening a differentiating claim is worse spent than the same effort buying availability and memory structures. In procurement-scripted enterprise sales, the RFP is a frame, usually written with an incumbent's help, and the choice is to influence the specification months earlier or to decline the deal — reframing in the response document is theatre. In markets moving faster than a sales cycle, occupying a position can be slower than the position decays. And most commonly: when retention is poor or distribution is absent, repositioning is a displacement activity that feels like strategy. A useful test is whether your best-retaining cohort is thriving. If existing customers who match your intended position are churning, the problem is not the frame.

5. Hard Edge Cases and the Organisational Seams

Multi-product portfolios. Once a company sells three products to overlapping buyers, it holds at least four positions: one per product, plus one for the company. The classic error is to let the company position be the union of the product positions, which produces the word "platform" and no meaning. The workable pattern is subordination: the company position asserts a single domain of competence, each product position asserts a specific alternative it displaces, and the two are allowed to differ in altitude without contradicting each other. The tell of a broken portfolio position is that the sales team leads with the company story in first meetings and the win rate on first meetings is materially below the win rate on meetings where a specific product was named in the calendar invitation.

Two-sided markets. A marketplace must position separately to supply and demand, and the two positions will be in tension because one side's gain is often framed as the other's cost. The specific failure is cross-side leakage: the supply-side pitch — "reach customers you cannot reach" — is visible to demand-side buyers on the same website, and tells them the marketplace's loyalty lies with sellers. Mature marketplaces solve this with separated surfaces and a single shared value claim expressed in different currencies. The harder structural point is that a marketplace's frame of reference on each side is usually a different thing entirely: for sellers, the alternative is a sales team or a distributor; for buyers, the alternative is calling three suppliers. Positioning that treats "the marketplace" as one product misses that the two frames barely touch.

Regulated products, where the category label is a legal fact. In India this is unusually consequential. Whether a product is positioned as a lender or as a technology service provider to a regulated lender determines the applicability of the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework. Whether a health product presents itself as a wellness application or as software with a diagnostic claim determines whether it falls within the medical device rules administered by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. Whether a distribution product is a broker or a corporate agent changes its obligations under the insurance regulator's rules. In these categories the marketing sentence and the licence application must agree, and product teams have written positioning statements that their own compliance functions could not sign. The discipline is simple and frequently skipped: every candidate category label goes past legal before it goes past the board.

Hardware plus software. Samarth's case is the archetype. Hardware is bought from capital budgets and depreciated; software and data services are bought from operating budgets and renewed. The frames attach to different ledgers with different approval thresholds, different seasonal rhythms and different owners. A reframe from hardware to service is therefore not a messaging change but a change in whose signature is required and when money is available — which is why such reframes so often work in pilots and stall at scale, because pilots are paid for out of discretionary funds that do not exist at volume. The channel compounds this. Distributors sell into the frame they already know; a distributor who has sold instruments for fifteen years will resell Samarth as an instrument no matter what the brochure says, because that is the buyer they have a relationship with. A reframe that the channel cannot execute is a reframe of the direct business only.

AI-native products. Here the frame choice has become unusually stark, because AI products can credibly be positioned against software or against labour, and the two frames are separated by an order of magnitude in price and in evidence burden. The labour frame sets the price ceiling at a wage bill or a services contract, which is enormous, and simultaneously sets the quality bar at human-comparable performance, which is exacting, and often implies an obligation — an accuracy commitment, an indemnity, an audit trail — that a software frame never demands. The software frame is safe, cheap to sell into and permanently capped. There is a third frame, the co-pilot inside an incumbent's application, which gets distribution and surrenders the roadmap, the pricing power and eventually the customer relationship to the host. Anirudh's decision is exactly a choice among these three, and there is no consensus answer in the field; the honest statement is that the labour frame has the higher ceiling and the higher variance.

6. The Nuances That Separate an Expert From a Competent Practitioner

The frame sets the price anchor before it sets the message, and the budget line is the real position. The obvious reading is that positioning influences pricing. The accurate reading is that the frame is the pricing decision, taken implicitly and usually by people who do not know they are taking it. The tell-tale sign in the wild is discounting that clusters unevenly: one segment closes at list, another at thirty per cent off, and nobody can articulate why. That pattern almost always means two frames are running concurrently and one of them has a cheap reference price. The diagnostic is to ask two account executives, separately, which line item the money comes out of. Different answers, different positions.

A frame must be cheap for the buyer to verify, not merely true. Competent practitioners choose the frame where their advantage is largest. Experts choose the frame where the ratio of advantage to verification cost is largest, which is often a different frame. The tell is a long, cheerful "education" phase in deals — champions who believe you, enjoy the conversation, and cannot re-narrate your argument to their CFO without you in the room. Every hour of buyer education is a cost you have transferred to the buyer, and buyers repay it in cycle time and in a higher probability of no-decision. The obvious reading — that education is investment — is wrong more often than it is right, because the education does not accumulate across buyers unless the frame is shared.

Choosing a frame is choosing whose feature table becomes your scoring rubric. This is the second-order effect experts watch most carefully, because it operates on the roadmap silently. The tell is a backlog with a visible stratum of parity items that no customer has ever used in anger but that three deals "required". The obvious reading is that these are competitive necessities. The accurate reading is that they are the tax you pay for sitting inside somebody else's frame, and their cost should be charged to the positioning decision rather than to engineering.

Category creation is a financed liability, not a communications choice. The competent practitioner treats "we are creating a new category" as a bold assertion. The expert treats it as a funding request with a measurable cost: the search volume that does not yet exist, the analyst coverage that must be purchased in attention over years, the procurement taxonomy that has no drawer for you, and a sales cycle stretched by the buyer's need to invent an internal justification. The tell is customer acquisition cost that refuses to improve as brand spend rises, combined with the sentence "we just need to educate the market" surviving into its fourth quarter. The obvious reading is that the category is taking time. The accurate reading is that the category is being funded out of a budget that was scoped for demand capture, not demand creation.

Positions have latency, and the latency is roughly your sales cycle multiplied by the number of touches needed to overwrite a memory. A team that reframes in January and sees no change by March concludes the reframe failed. What has actually happened is that the pipeline in March was created under the old frame. The tell is closed-won notes still citing the old comparison two quarters after launch. The expert instruments this explicitly — tagging opportunities by the frame in force when they were created — and refuses to judge a reframe on cohorts that predate it. Reading the reframe as a failure and reverting is the single most expensive unforced error in this topic, because it converts one slow reframe into two.

A position that forbids nothing is not a position. The purpose of choosing a frame is to make some requests obviously out of scope. The tell is an executive team that cannot, on the spot, name three things it will refuse to build. The obvious reading of a broad position is that it preserves optionality. The accurate reading is that it exports the prioritisation problem to whoever shouts loudest, usually the largest current customer, and that the resulting roadmap will be a weighted average of other companies' strategies.

"Who cares a lot" is a claim about the gradient of value, not the size of the segment. The competent practitioner picks the biggest addressable segment. The expert picks the segment where willingness-to-pay changes most steeply with the specific thing they are good at, even when that segment is small, because a steep gradient produces price realisation, fast decisions and referenceable outcomes, and because segments with steep gradients are where a defensible position can be held while the company is still small. The tell of getting this wrong is a large target market with a flat, low, remarkably consistent willingness to pay — the signature of a commodity in disguise.

Positioning against non-consumption is legitimate and distorts every metric you use to manage. If the alternative is a spreadsheet, an intern or nothing, win rates look extraordinary because you are rarely in a competitive evaluation; cycle times look terrible because there is no budget line waiting; and churn is deferred rather than avoided, surfacing at the first renewal when the customer reassesses a habit they never fully formed. The tell is a high win rate coexisting with a high no-decision rate. The obvious reading is that sales is executing well. The accurate reading is that the funnel's arithmetic has been changed by the frame and the dashboards have not been re-baselined.

Repositioning rides on forcing events; announcements alone rarely move a market. Experts time a reframe to coincide with something the market must attend to anyway — a pricing change, a new product, a funding round, a regulatory shift, an acquisition. The reason is mechanical: a buyer's mental model is updated when it is already being accessed. The tell of the amateur version is a repositioning executed as a website change and an internal all-hands, with no change to price, packaging, sales compensation or the first slide of the deck. If the compensation plan did not change, the position did not change.

Accepting the incumbent's frame and winning inside it is sometimes the highest-return move, and reframing is over-prescribed. This is the nuance that most distinguishes experienced operators, because the literature is written by people who reframe for a living. When a frame is well-established, has budget attached, has procurement categories and analyst coverage, and your product is genuinely better on the criteria that frame makes salient, then reframing throws away free demand in exchange for the privilege of a fight you must finance. The tell that you should stay is a healthy win rate against named competitors combined with a shortage of pipeline: that is a distribution problem wearing a positioning costume. The expert's question is not "what frame makes us look best" but "what frame makes us look best per rupee of demand creation we must fund".

7. How It Differs Across Product Types and Stages — and Where It Does Not

The mechanism is invariant: a buyer compares, and the comparison set determines the verdict. What varies is who holds the frame, how fast it changes, and how expensive it is to move.

Two stage-related points deserve emphasis because they are frequently inverted. First, early-stage companies are told to position sharply, and should, but they hold the weakest evidence for doing so; the honest practice is to write the position as a dated hypothesis with the specific observation that would refute it, and to revisit it every quarter until retention data can adjudicate. Second, late-stage companies are told that repositioning is hard because markets have long memories. The larger constraint is internal: an installed base has been sold a promise, a sales force has been compensated against a motion, and a services organisation has been staffed to a scope. Repositioning at scale is an operations programme with a communications component, not the reverse.

8. Three Worked Examples, Including One That Failed

8.1 Samarth Instruments: a reframe tested before it was announced

Devika did something unusual before the September board meeting: she ran the reframe as an experiment rather than as a launch. Between 1 July and 22 August 2025, her team took eighteen qualified opportunities and split them. Nine were pursued as instruments — datasheet, spec comparison, plant head. Nine were pursued as residual-value assurance — a two-page retrospective analysis of the prospect's own repossessed or retired vehicles, presented to a risk or finance owner, with the SX-40 introduced only as the means of data collection.

Two findings mattered more than the headline. The first was that the retrospective analysis — running Samarth's model backwards over vehicles the prospect had already disposed of — solved the verification problem identified in condition C2, converting a claim that would otherwise take months to prove into a claim provable in an afternoon with the buyer's own data. The second was that in three of the nine Frame B deals, the plant head who would have been the buyer in Frame A became an active obstacle, because the reframe implied that his replacement rule of thumb had been costing the company money. Reframes create losers inside the buyer's organisation, and the expert practice is to identify who, in advance, and to give them something.

8.2 Sanchika Fresh: a reframe that failed, and what the recovery cost

Sanchika Fresh began in 2021 as a weekly vegetable subscription in Pune: a fixed box delivered on Tuesdays and Fridays, sourced from a cluster of farms near Junnar, priced at ₹740 a week. By early 2024 it had 11,400 active subscribers, a customer acquisition cost of ₹640, monthly churn of 4.1 per cent, and a contribution margin of ₹96 per box. It was, by the standards of Indian consumer subscription businesses, unglamorous and working.

In April 2024, following a funding conversation in which an investor observed that vegetable delivery was a crowded frame occupied by much larger players, the founders repositioned Sanchika Fresh as "India's preventive-health food platform". The product barely changed. The website, the packaging, the app onboarding and the performance-marketing creative all changed. The category claim moved from "vegetable box" to "preventive health".

Three things went wrong, and they are worth separating because they have different lessons. First, the new frame had no existing demand: nobody searches for a preventive-health food platform, so paid acquisition had to create the need and satisfy it in the same session, which tripled the cost per acquisition. Second, the new frame raised expectations the product did not meet — subscribers who joined for preventive health expected nutritionist guidance and personalisation, received a vegetable box, and churned at nearly twice the previous rate. This is the mechanism by which a reframe can destroy retention without touching the product: retention is measured against the promise, and the promise had moved. Third, the reframe was chosen to impress a capital provider rather than a buyer — the frame was optimised for the wrong audience, which is the specific pathology of investor-facing positioning.

The recovery, begun in January 2025, is instructive because it was not a simple reversal. The founders returned to the vegetable frame but narrowed it rather than restoring it: "the Tuesday and Friday box that has never missed a delivery in three years", with reliability as the point of difference and on-time percentage published on the landing page. That claim sat inside an existing frame with existing demand, was verifiable in one glance, and was true — Sanchika's route density in three Pune corridors genuinely produced a delivery reliability its larger competitors could not match citywide. Conversion recovered above its original level, churn fell below it, and contribution per box rose because reliability supported a modest price increase. The lesson is not that the company should never have repositioned. It is that the original frame was not exhausted; it had simply never been sharpened.

8.3 Saumitra Legal Intelligence: pricing the frame before choosing it

Anirudh's team ran a narrower experiment in August and September 2025: they took the same eleven prospects and, at the first meeting, asked a single question before any pitch — "if you did not solve this with software, what would you do?" Seven named an outsourced review vendor or additional headcount. Four named an existing legal technology suite. The seven were then pursued in the labour frame, with a blind benchmark offered on five hundred already-reviewed contracts. Four converted to paid pilots at an average of ₹41 lakh, against an average of ₹12 lakh for the pilots sold in the software frame — but two of the four demanded an accuracy commitment with financial consequence, and Saumitra's answer on both was a capped service credit rather than an indemnity, which cost it one of the two.

The instructive number was not the price. It was the gross margin. Contracts sold in the labour frame at ₹41 lakh carried inference and human-review costs of about ₹9 lakh, giving 78 per cent margin; contracts sold in the software frame at ₹12 lakh carried nearly identical absolute costs of ₹6.2 lakh, giving 48 per cent. The frame determined not only revenue but the ratio of price to a largely fixed delivery cost, which is the single most important sentence in this section for anyone running an AI-native product. When your cost of delivery is roughly invariant to the frame and your price is not, the frame choice is the margin structure of the business.

9. Failure Modes, Their Early Warnings and the Cost of Late Diagnosis

The half-life problem deserves separate treatment because it has become acute. A differentiating attribute has a decay curve: the interval between your claim and competitor parity. In stable software markets that interval historically ran two to four years. In AI-native products through 2024 and 2025, teams have repeatedly found it running two to four quarters. The practical consequence is that attribute-level positioning in fast-moving categories must be treated as a depreciating asset, and the durable positions are built on things that decay slowly — accumulated proprietary data, a workflow the customer has configured, an obligation you have taken on that rivals will not, a distribution relationship. Devika's residual-value model is, in this light, attractive not because the analytics are clever but because eleven months of Indian pack telemetry cannot be acquired in a quarter by anyone.

10. Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

Four disagreements are live, consequential and not resolvable by appeal to evidence currently available. They are stated here in their strongest form, because the practitioner's job is to know which one they are in.

Does differentiated positioning drive choice at all? The Ehrenberg-Bass position, steelmanned, is not that positioning is unimportant but that the mechanism marketers believe in is wrong: buyers in established categories are largely habitual, brands within a category share buyers in proportion to their size, and growth comes overwhelmingly from penetration driven by mental availability across many category entry points, not from persuasion by a differentiating argument. The evidence is strong and unusually general — the double jeopardy and duplication-of-purchase regularities replicate across hundreds of categories over decades. For this position to be wrong in a given case, you would need to show a market where buyers genuinely deliberate, where switching costs or considered purchase make the comparison explicit, and where the difference is verifiable at the moment of choice. That description fits most B2B purchases above a few lakh rupees and fits almost no consumer packaged goods purchase. The reason competent people talk past each other here is that they are generalising from different halves of the economy.

Can a firm create a category, or are categories conferred by buyers? The category-design school points to the observable concentration of value in firms that named a problem and became its reference implementation, and argues that the alternative — positioning against incumbents — permanently cedes the evaluation criteria. The sceptical position is that the sample is contaminated by survivorship: for every firm that created a category, some large and unmeasured number spent their runway funding a drawer in the buyer's filing cabinet that never got used, and that the observed successes were mostly firms that found a category already forming and named it first. What would have to be true for the category-design school to be wrong is that the base rate of successful category creation, measured across all attempts rather than across the survivors, is low relative to the base rate of winning inside an existing frame with comparable capital. Nobody has that denominator, which is why the argument does not resolve.

Is the frame chosen or structurally determined? Porter's heirs argue that a position is a location within an industry structure and is sustainable only when an activity system is configured to it — meaning that a firm cannot simply elect a frame, because frames impose cost structures, capability requirements and trade-offs. Dunford's heirs argue that in technology markets, where the same underlying capability can be configured for radically different buyers, the frame is genuinely elective and the activity system follows. Both are right about different firms. The practical test is whether serving the new frame requires assets you do not have and cannot buy: for Samarth, actuarial capability and an accuracy obligation; for Saumitra, an insurance-backed commitment. If the answer is yes and the acquisition path is unclear, the structuralists are describing your situation.

For AI-native products: labour frame or software frame? The labour frame's advocates note that the price ceiling is set by a wage bill rather than a software budget, that the buyer's willingness to pay is anchored to a number ten to fifty times larger, and that this is the only frame in which the economics of AI products make sense at scale. The software frame's advocates note that the labour frame imports a quality bar calibrated to a human professional, an implicit obligation for errors, a procurement process designed for services vendors, and a political problem inside the customer that no software sale has to survive. The evidence at present is genuinely mixed: the highest contract values are being achieved in the labour frame and so are the longest sales cycles and the most expensive failures. The honest summary is that this is a variance decision as much as a mean decision, and a firm's balance sheet and risk appetite should inform it more than its ambition does.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has merely studied positioning produces a well-formed statement, presents it, and treats the exercise as complete. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in six observable ways.

They ask about the buyer's alternative before they say anything about their own product, in every first meeting, and they treat the answer as data rather than as an objection to be handled. They know, without checking, which budget line their last ten deals were paid from, because they have asked. They can name the three things their position forbids them from building, and they have said no to a large customer on that basis within the last year. They treat a reframe as an operations programme — pricing, packaging, compensation, hiring, channel enablement, analyst briefings — and they can say which of those they have not yet done. They instrument the reframe by tagging opportunities with the frame in force at creation, so that they never judge a new position on old pipeline. And they are willing to say, in a room that wants a bold answer, that the existing frame is fine and the problem is distribution — which is the least popular correct answer in this subject and the one that most reliably distinguishes judgement from enthusiasm.

One further tell: masters hold their position loosely at the level of words and tightly at the level of the comparison. They will let sales rephrase the sentence a dozen ways. They will not let anyone quietly change which alternative the buyer is being asked to reject, because that is the decision, and everything else is phrasing.

12. What They Decided

Devika took a split proposal to the September board. Samarth would continue to sell the SX-40 as an instrument through its distribution channel, unchanged, because that business funded the plant and because the channel could not execute anything else. In parallel, a separate ten-person unit — two actuarial hires, four data engineers, three risk-facing sales people and a product manager — would sell residual-value assurance direct to NBFCs and large fleet financiers, priced as an annual subscription per financed vehicle, with the SX-40 supplied as instrumentation rather than sold. Her reasoning rested on Table 4's pre-sales engineering figure: the reframe was worth roughly twenty times per opportunity but consumed seven times the engineering, and attempting it across the whole business would have starved both. She also insisted on one condition the board resisted: the new unit would not be allowed to quote an instrument price, ever, because a single quotation in the old frame would reset the anchor for the whole account.

Anirudh moved the 1 November price list to the labour frame, but not entirely. Saumitra would price per contract reviewed, with a floor commitment, explicitly benchmarked against the client's current outsourced cost — and would offer a capped service credit rather than an indemnity, accepting that this would lose some deals. He kept a smaller, self-serve, seat-priced product in the software frame, positioned deliberately as an entry point rather than as the main business, with a migration path priced to make the move attractive. His reasoning was the gross-margin observation: with delivery costs roughly invariant to frame, the labour frame was the only one in which Saumitra could fund the accuracy work that the labour frame demanded. He was explicit with his board that this was the higher-variance choice and that the accuracy commitment was the thing most likely to break it.

Discussion questions.

1. Devika's paired test showed a twentyfold difference in expected value per opportunity, yet she chose to keep the instrument business intact and run the reframe in a separate unit. Was this prudent sequencing or an expensive hedge that will leave Samarth stuck between two frames? What evidence, available in the next two quarters, would settle it?

2. Sanchika Fresh's recovery narrowed the original frame rather than restoring it. Under what conditions is sharpening an existing frame strictly superior to moving to a new one — and how would a founder tell, before spending the money, which situation they are in?

3. Anirudh accepts a higher-variance position because it is the only one whose margins fund the quality bar it imposes. Is that reasoning sound, or is it a circular justification in which the frame creates the obligation that the frame is then needed to pay for?

13. Going Deeper

  • Competitive analysis — supplies the raw material: the actual alternative set, sourced from transaction evidence rather than from a competitor deck. Without it, every frame you choose is a guess dressed as a decision.
  • Blue Ocean and category creation — the strongest form of the "create your own frame" argument, with the strategy canvas as its working tool. Read it against the survivorship critique in section 10.
  • Product–market–channel fit — explains why a reframe the channel cannot execute is only a reframe of the direct business, and why distribution capability constrains which frames are actually available to you.
  • Writing a positioning statement — the craft of compressing the decision into a sentence a champion can forward. Useful only after the frame is chosen; done first, it manufactures confidence.
  • What pricing signals — price is the loudest positioning claim you make, and the one buyers trust most. Unlocks the discipline of checking that price and frame agree.
  • Relaunching and repositioning an existing product — the operations programme behind a frame change: migration, compensation, packaging, analyst briefing. The Sanchika Fresh example is a case study in what it costs to skip it.
  • Right to win — forces the honest question behind condition C3: is the strength you are framing around actually unequally distributed, or merely present?
  • Moats and the 7 Powers — supplies the vocabulary for which positions are defensible over time, and separates attribute claims from structural ones as in Figure 3.
  • Network effects — the case where the frame changes as you grow, because the alternative set a buyer considers shrinks as the network thickens; positioning becomes partly endogenous.
  • Switching costs and lock-in — determines whether a buyer's existing frame is merely familiar or economically binding, which changes whether reframing is persuasion or futility.
  • Moats in the AI era — directly relevant to the half-life problem: which advantages still decay slowly when capability diffuses in quarters rather than years.
  • Five forces and industry structure — the structuralist counterweight to elective framing, and the discipline that tells you when a frame your cost structure cannot serve is a fantasy rather than a choice.

Positioning at Gathri Spend Systems

Bengaluru, 14 September 2026

1. Opening

Ananya Krishnan, chief product officer of Gathri Spend Systems, closed her laptop at nine in the evening and looked at the calendar on her desk. Nine days remained until the board meeting at which the company's Series B narrative would be locked, and eleven days until the renewal call with Girnar Freight Exchange, a Dubai-based logistics group and Gathri's largest single account. Both needed the same thing by Friday: one settled answer to the question marketing, sales and the website vendor had all been asking for six weeks — what category should Gathri say it is in? The website, the sales deck and the board narrative could not each tell a different story. Ananya had the data to make the call. What she lacked was agreement from the three colleagues who would have to live with it.

2. Company background

Gathri Spend Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by Vikram Sethi, previously a product manager at Razorpay, to solve a problem he had lived with directly: mid-sized Indian companies reimbursed employee expenses through email chains and spreadsheets, and finance teams spent days each month reconciling them. Gathri began as reimbursement software, added a corporate card programme in 2021 through a scheduled bank partner operating under the Reserve Bank of India's co-branded card and prepaid instrument guidelines, and by 2023 had layered a spend-analytics dashboard on top — built first for its own finance team, then opened to customers almost as an afterthought. Today it serves 260 customers across India, the UAE and Singapore, from hundred-person startups to logistics and manufacturing groups with thousands of employees. It is not alone. Enkash, Happay and Zaggle issue corporate cards to similar customers and compete hard on interchange sharing; Zoho Expense, bundled into the widely used Zoho One suite, and SAP Concur at the enterprise end compete on expense workflow. Gathri has always described itself as the third kind of company: smart corporate cards for growing businesses. Exhibit 1 sets out where that business stands today.

3. The situation

Growth had not stopped, but its shape had changed. In the mid-market segment, Enkash and Happay were undercutting Gathri on card economics, and deals that once closed in three weeks now dragged into negotiations over basis points of interchange sharing. In the enterprise segment the pattern was different and, to Ananya, more interesting. Priyanka Iyer, the data science lead working out of Toronto, had pulled twelve months of usage logs and found that among enterprise accounts, 61 per cent of monthly active use was on the spend-analytics dashboard, 27 per cent on card transactions, and 12 per cent on the reimbursement workflow that had once been the whole product. Divya Ramaswamy, the customer-success lead in Singapore, had been hearing the same thing directly from clients: finance controllers who had used Gathri for a year would ask, almost by accident, whether it could flag a vendor whose invoices were rising faster than volume — not realising the anomaly-detection feature they wanted already existed, because no one had told them it was a headline capability rather than a minor add-on. Rohan Vaidya, head of sales in Edison, New Jersey, who managed large diaspora-founded accounts across the Gulf and North America, saw the cost from the other side: pitched as a card issuer to a CFO who already had a banking relationship for cards, the conversation stalled on price; demonstrated as an analytics dashboard, it moved to value. The Girnar Freight Exchange renewal made the stakes concrete. Girnar ran freight operations across India and the UAE, held an annual contract worth ₹1.6 crore, and had told Divya plainly that it stayed for the spend-visibility dashboard its finance director used every week — not the cards, which its treasury team barely touched. Exhibit 2 lays out, across four quarters of competitive deals, how differently the three possible frames performed.

4. The people

Ananya Krishnan — Chief product officer, Bengaluru. Owns the decision and must make website, sales deck and board narrative agree within nine days. Wants a frame that stays true for years, not one re-explained every quarter.

Vikram Sethi — Founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Needs a category story Series B investors will recognise as large and defensible, not a niche feature description.

Rohan Vaidya — Head of sales, Edison, New Jersey. Wants to keep the card frame because it is a fifteen-minute pitch that closes fast against Enkash and Happay, and worries a new category lengthens every cycle he owns.

Divya Ramaswamy — Customer success lead, Singapore. Wants the spend-intelligence frame made explicit, since it is what keeps accounts like Girnar renewing and what her team could expand, if only marketing named it.

6. The options

Option A: Stay a corporate card issuer. Keep the current frame and keep competing head-to-head with Enkash, Happay and Zaggle on interchange sharing, with the analytics dashboard mentioned late, if at all, in the sales cycle. The upside is a category CFOs already budget for and a sales motion Rohan's team already runs at speed. The cost, visible in Exhibit 2, is a 35 per cent win rate, a ₹9 lakh average deal, and a segment where price is the only lever left.

Option B: Reposition as a spend-intelligence platform for finance teams. Make analytics the headline across website, sales deck and board narrative, with card issuance and reimbursement presented as the data sources that feed it. The upside, again from Exhibit 2, is a ₹34 lakh average deal and no named direct competitor, matching what usage data and the Girnar renewal already say about where the value sits. The cost is today's lower win rate (15 per cent, on a frame barely tested), a longer buyer-education cycle, and a pricing model that can no longer lean on interchange alone.

Option C: Run two frames in parallel. Keep the card-issuer story for self-serve, price-sensitive mid-market customers, and use the spend-intelligence story only above an enterprise deal-size threshold. The upside is protecting near-term mid-market revenue while giving enterprise reps a sharper story. The cost is that Gathri would be telling customers and investors two different accounts of what kind of company it is — the split that positioning theory warns against, since a company is only ever obviously strong in one frame of reference at a time.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 reveal about the frame in which Gathri's strengths are obvious, as distinct from the frame its marketing uses today?
  2. How should Ananya weigh a 15 per cent win rate on an untested frame against a 45 per cent win rate on a frame visibly losing ground on price?
  3. What does Girnar's stated reason for renewing tell Ananya about which alternative Gathri is really being compared against, in the customer's own mind?
  4. Is Option C a genuine third path, or does it avoid the choice positioning requires Ananya to make?

8. A note for the learner

Positioning, in April Dunford's sense, is not a slogan-writing exercise; it is the choice of a frame of reference — a category, a set of alternatives, an idea of who the buyer compares you to — inside which your genuine strengths are the obvious, decisive ones. The frame is chosen relative to alternatives a buyer already holds in mind, which is why competitive analysis has to come first: Gathri's problem was never a lack of strength, but a mismatch between where its strength actually lived (spend intelligence, per Exhibits 1 and 2) and the frame it had used since 2021 (corporate cards, where it is one of several similarly priced options).

A well-reasoned answer takes Exhibit 2 seriously rather than defensively: a 15 per cent win rate on the spend-intelligence frame is not evidence the frame fails, it is evidence the frame has never been properly pitched, packaged or priced — every one of those 40 deals was an improvisation. A weaker answer treats Option C as a safe compromise; a careful reader notices it is not a compromise at all, but a decision to remain positioned nowhere in particular — still visible in the market map's dashed circle, sitting between two clusters it does not belong to.

The defensible path is Option B, taken deliberately rather than abruptly: lead the website, sales deck and board narrative with spend intelligence for finance teams as the category, retire card-issuer framing as the headline while keeping cards and reimbursement as the product's data-gathering engine rather than its identity, and give Rohan's team a properly built version of the pitch his reps were already improvising with the best results per deal. The near-term cost — a slower mid-market motion while buyers learn the frame, and pricing rebuilt around analytics value rather than interchange — is the price of a frame in which Gathri's strength is obvious, not merely present.

Taraazu Water Systems: Which Business Are We In?

Pune, Tuesday 29 September 2026, 10.40 p.m.

1. The night before

The rain had stopped over Baner an hour earlier, and from the third floor of Taraazu Water Systems’ office Sharvari Godbole could hear the storm drain carrying away more water in an hour than any customer of hers would buy in a month. Three documents were open in front of her. Thursday’s board pack, slide four still titled, in the placeholder grey her designer in Berlin used for unapproved text, Taraazu is the category leader in ____. A term sheet from Tapti Growth Capital: ₹150 crore of Series B money at a pre-money valuation of ₹520 crore, with a note saying the investment committee “needs to hear one sentence about what market this is, not three”. And a memo from Dubai, where Tazkia Industrial Services LLC wanted its ₹2.85 crore annual contract restructured around quarterly water-stewardship reporting rather than around meters.

Sharvari had spent nine years certain that Taraazu measured water better than anyone in the country. What she was no longer certain of was the sentence that followed. At nine the next morning she and Aniruddh Kelkar, her co-founder and chief executive, would agree the frame in which Taraazu would ask the board, the fund and its customers to judge it. Nothing in her data made the choice obvious; too much in it made three different choices defensible.

2. How Taraazu got here

Taraazu was founded in Pune in 2017 by Aniruddh, a mechanical engineer who had spent eleven years designing water-treatment skids, and Sharvari, then a plant-instrumentation specialist. Their first product was an ultrasonic bulk-flow meter, ruggedised for the muddy, chlorinated, intermittent supply of Indian industrial estates. It worked where imported meters silted up, and by 2019 the company had a reputation among plant utilities engineers as the outfit whose meters did not lie.

That reputation produced the decision that still constrains the company. In 2019 Taraazu won a tender funded under the central government’s AMRUT programme to install 40,000 domestic meters for a Maharashtra municipal corporation. The board believed municipal metering was the growth engine: volumes were enormous, the Jal Jeevan Mission was pouring money into water infrastructure, and every meter was an annuity of data. Nobody modelled the receivable. Payments ran eleven to fourteen months behind delivery, working capital was financed against Aniruddh’s personal guarantee, and Taraazu left municipal work in 2021 having written off ₹4.8 crore.

The lesson the founders drew was never again to carry the cost of reaching customers themselves. In April 2022 they signed a five-year exclusive distribution agreement with Trishool Industrial Supply Co., a Rajkot distributor of pumps and instrumentation with 340 dealers across western and southern India. Sales cost fell immediately. Two other things happened that nobody wrote down. The agreement defined Taraazu’s products, for purposes of exclusivity, as “metering and instrumentation goods and any software supplied therewith”, with a right of first refusal over that definition until 31 March 2028. And 340 dealers began describing Taraazu to every factory manager in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu as a meter company — which is what the market now believes.

The software came anyway. In 2023 Taraazu launched Flow, a subscription dashboard turning meter data into baselines, leak alerts and effluent-recovery recommendations, and in 2024 Ila Mukherjee, hired in Toronto because nobody in Pune would take the role at the salary offered, built the savings model quoted in every deck since. Then, in January 2025, water intensity became a number audit committees had to defend, and enquiries began arriving from sustainability heads rather than plant engineers. Nobody had built a product for them; Sohini Dasgupta, who runs marketing from Bengaluru, wrote a pitch deck anyway.

3. The industry

India’s industrial water market has no tidy boundary, which is precisely Sharvari’s problem. At one edge sit equipment and treatment companies — Thermax, Ion Exchange, VA Tech Wabag, Grundfos — for whom measurement is an accessory to capital plant. At another sit meter manufacturers, where volume producers have pushed a basic mechanical meter to a price at which no software business can be funded; Genus Power and its peers have shown in electricity what smart-metering scale does to margins. At a third sit energy-services firms and consultants who sell guaranteed savings for a share of the reduction, and who hold the plant relationships Taraazu reaches only through Trishool’s dealers. At a fourth, newest edge sit sustainability-reporting platforms, mostly carbon-first, for whom water is a thin module and whose buyers sit in corporate offices.

Regulation pushes in several directions at once. Central Ground Water Authority permissions and pollution control board consents make water a licence-to-operate issue for a paper mill or a dye house. The Legal Metrology Act governs what a meter must be certified to do if a bill is raised on its reading, which keeps the hardware line expensive and slow to change. SEBI’s assurance requirement makes water a boardroom issue for the largest listed companies only. Tazkia, with six industrial laundries and two beverage plants across Dubai and Sharjah, answers to its parent’s disclosure obligations and to a tariff several times the Indian industrial rate. And the weather intrudes: deficient monsoons in 2023 and 2024 made scarcity a board topic in western Maharashtra, while a generous 2026 monsoon has pushed three prospects into the next year.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Taraazu closed FY26, the year to 31 March 2026, at ₹65 crore of revenue, up from ₹52 crore — growth of 25 per cent, and the first year in which the founders had to explain why a software company earned three-fifths of its money from hardware. Exhibit 1 sets out the mix, and the margin gap inside it between the ₹39.00 crore of meters sold through Trishool and the ₹16.25 crore of Flow subscriptions.

Through 2025 the belief was that metering bought distribution, subscriptions bought margin, and the two would converge as meters became the data layer under Flow. Exhibit 3 is where that belief began coming apart. Of 1,200 sites surveyed in FY26, 240 started a paid pilot — 240 of 1,200, or 20 per cent. Of those, 132 reached a verified savings report, but only 66 of the 240 pilots converted into an annual subscription, which is 27.5 per cent, and 51 of the 66 renewed at twelve months. The pilots did not fail for want of leaks to find. They failed, according to Kashvi Trivedi’s interviews in Singapore, because the engineer who signed the pilot had no budget beyond maintenance, and whoever could act on the report had never been in the room.

Then came the savings problem. Ila’s model, trained on 2023–24 data from fourteen paper and pulp sites, underpinned the claim of “up to 19 per cent water savings”. In February 2026 the engineering team audited the 66 converted sites against metered consumption before and after. Exhibit 4 sets them side by side: the modelled saving averaged 13.9 per cent, the median validated saving 5.3 per cent. Ila has been precise about the divergence: the model assumed a detected leak was repaired within thirty days, where the median repair interval at a textile site was ninety-four days and 31 per cent of flagged leaks were never closed. Whether that is a flaw in the model or in the product she and the field-operations head in Coimbatore have not settled.

Against that, Exhibit 2 arrived like a gift. Deals pitched as water risk and disclosure closed at 45 per cent, with an average first-year value of ₹72.0 lakh against ₹19.0 lakh for a metering-led deal, and Exhibit 5 makes the contrast starker still. What neither exhibit says on its face is that there were only 20 such opportunities, every one inbound, most arriving after a BRSR assurance consultant mentioned Taraazu by name. Nobody has sold it cold. In August, Taraazu lost two efficiency-led deals at Tamil Nadu dyeing units to a bidder offering a savings-share contract with a floor guarantee.

5. The people

Sharvari Godbole — Co-founder and head of product, Pune. Believes the frame must follow the strength, and the strength is measurement nobody disputes. Not saying: she wrote the page carrying the 19 per cent claim, which an outcome-based frame would put under audit.

Aniruddh Kelkar — Co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Will take whichever frame closes the Series B by December; the round retires his 2019 personal guarantee. Not saying: he has already told Tapti that disclosure is where Taraazu is going.

Nachiket Bhave — Vice-president, hardware and operations, Pune. Argues Taraazu is a metering company that happens to sell software, and 340 dealers are a moat; his 90-person field organisation lives on meter volumes. Not saying: Trishool’s general manager has hinted that a move away from instrumentation would breach the exclusivity’s spirit.

Sohini Dasgupta — Head of marketing, Bengaluru. Wants Taraazu to own water risk and disclosure before a carbon platform adds a water module; her ₹4.10 crore budget is justifiable only for a category story. Not saying: two of the nine disclosure wins came from one consultant, secured by no contract.

Harish Iyengar — Head of enterprise sales, Edison, New Jersey, covering the Gulf and North America. Says disclosure is unproven and metering is dying, and only efficiency has cold-outbound evidence; his quota rests on a 58-deal metering base. Not saying: his largest FY27 commission line is the Tazkia renewal, which he thinks he can save only by promising reporting Taraazu cannot yet deliver.

Ila Mukherjee — Senior data scientist, Toronto. Insists the model is sound and the execution gap is the customer’s. Not saying: the version she is drafting would put the defensible sector average nearer 7 per cent, making any savings guarantee uninsurable.

Kashvi Trivedi — Customer success lead, Singapore. Reports that renewals correlate with whether a sustainability head, rather than a plant engineer, sponsored the account. Not saying, except in a footnote: her sample is 51 renewals.

Legal Metrology approvals delay any change to billing-grade meters by nine to twelve months. The disclosure team is four people; the two senior hires Sohini wants cost ₹1.1 crore a year in Berlin or Toronto bands against ₹32 lakh in Pune, and the candidates she wants are not in Pune. And SEBI’s assurance requirement, the engine under the disclosure frame, currently bites only for the largest listed companies — of Taraazu’s 88 FY26 wins, 6 were listed entities in that bracket.

  1. In which frame of reference are Taraazu's strengths obvious, and is that the frame its revenue currently sits in? Use Exhibits 1, 2 and 5 rather than the founders' assertions.

  5. Is the Trishool agreement a moat, a constraint, or the reason the market’s frame for Taraazu is already fixed? What would you give up to reopen it?
  6. All four options assume one category for one company. If that framing is wrong, what is the better question — and what should Sharvari do at nine on Monday morning, and say to the board on Thursday?

11. Later that night

At 11.20 p.m. Sharvari did the arithmetic she had been avoiding. Nine disclosure wins, every one handed to the company by somebody else. Fifty-eight metering wins, each earning less than a lakh of contribution in its first year. Twenty-one efficiency wins resting on a number her own data scientist would not sign. She opened the board pack, deleted the placeholder on slide four, typed Taraazu is the category leader in and stopped, because she did not know whether the sentence described the company she had, the company she wanted, or the company Deven needed. Outside, the storm drain was still running.
