Positioning: In Which Frame of Reference Are Your Strengths Obvious?

Meera Iyer has a product that works. What she does not yet have is a sentence that tells a cardiologist in Nashik, in the eleven seconds before he stops listening, why Prakhar HealthOS is the thing he should buy instead of the thing he is already doing.

1. A Tuesday in Bengaluru

On the second Tuesday of March 2024, Meera Iyer, VP of Product at Prakhar HealthOS, sat in a glass-walled conference room on the fourth floor of a co-working tower in HSR Layout, staring at a funnel report that did not make sense. Prakhar HealthOS sold software that helped diabetes and hypertension clinics track patients between visits — medication reminders, blood-pressure and blood-sugar logging via a patient app, and a dashboard that flagged which patients were drifting out of control so a nurse could call them before a crisis, not after one. The company had sixty-one clinics live, roughly fourteen crore rupees in annual recurring revenue, and a Series B closing in eleven weeks that depended on proving the sales motion was repeatable. It was not proving repeatable. The sales team was closing deals, but the deals that closed fastest were the smallest, and the deals that mattered — hundred-plus-doctor hospital chains — were stalling for months and then evaporating.

Two conversations from the previous week explained why, though Meera had not yet connected them. In the first, a procurement head at a fourteen-hospital chain in Nashik had asked Prakhar's account executive, not unkindly, "So this is like an EMR, but for chronic patients only? Because we already have Pinaki MedSystems installed across all our wards, and their new module does patient reminders too." In the second, the head nurse at a twelve-doctor diabetes clinic in Indore had said, "We already do this. I have two coordinators who call every patient with a home-glucose reading over 180. It works fine. Why would I pay you ₹149 a month per patient when Prerna CareLine charges us eighteen rupees a call and I only need four calls a month?" Two prospects, two entirely different objections, and Prakhar's own sales deck answered neither, because the deck described what the product did — track, remind, flag, escalate — without ever saying what it should be judged against. Meera's product was being evaluated three different ways by three different buyers, and in every one of those evaluations, someone else's strengths looked obvious and Prakhar's did not. If she could not fix that before the Series B data room closed, the round itself was at risk, because a growth-stage investor reads a stalling enterprise pipeline as a market-fit problem, not a sales-execution problem — and by April they would be right to.

2. The Idea

Positioning is the act of choosing the frame of reference in which a buyer evaluates your product — the specific set of alternatives, the specific category label, and the specific dimension of comparison — such that your product's actual strengths become the obvious criteria for the decision, rather than criteria on which a competitor happens to win. It is not a tagline, a slogan, or a paragraph of marketing copy; those are downstream expressions of a positioning choice that has already been made, well or badly, whether anyone said it out loud or not. The clearest modern articulation of this comes from April Dunford, a Toronto-based positioning consultant who spent two decades running product marketing inside enterprise software companies before codifying her method in the 2019 book Obviously Awesome. Dunford built on a much older idea — Al Ries and Jack Trout had argued in 1981's Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind that a product's position exists in the customer's head, not in the product itself, and that the fight for market leadership is fought there — but Dunford's contribution was to turn that insight into a repeatable, ten-component process that a product or founding team could actually run in a room in an afternoon, rather than leaving it to instinct or to whichever executive spoke last in the meeting.

The problem positioning was invented to solve is this: every product has multiple true things that could be said about it, and every buyer has multiple ways they could choose to compare it to alternatives, and most of those combinations make the product look mediocre. A diabetes-coordination platform compared against a full hospital EMR looks thin — it does not do billing, does not do inpatient records, does not integrate with insurance claims. The same platform compared against two nurses making phone calls with a spreadsheet looks expensive and complicated for what it does. Only when compared against a third frame — the cost and consequence of a preventable hospital readmission — does its actual advantage, continuous risk detection between visits, become the natural, load-bearing criterion. Positioning is the discipline of finding that third frame deliberately, before the market finds the wrong one for you by default. The sentence Meera needed to be able to say in a room, without sounding glib, was something close to: "We are not judged against EMRs or against call centres — we are the layer that catches a patient's blood-sugar spiral three weeks before it becomes a ₹40,000 hospital admission, and that is the only frame in which our accuracy and speed actually matter."

Positioning: choosing the specific competitive alternative, category, and buyer dimension against which your product is evaluated, so that its real advantages become the obvious basis for the decision.

3. How It Actually Works

Dunford's method proceeds in a fixed order, and the order matters, because each step constrains the ones that follow. Most teams get it backwards — they pick a category first, because a category is what goes on a homepage, and then they try to retrofit differentiation and buyers to fit a label they chose for aesthetic reasons. Positioning done properly starts at the other end, with the alternatives a real buyer would actually consider if your product did not exist, and builds the category last, as a conclusion rather than a starting assumption.

The first step is to list the competitive alternatives honestly — not just the named competitors that show up in analyst reports, but everything a buyer would do in your absence, including "nothing," "a spreadsheet," "an intern," or "the module our existing vendor already sells us." Meera's team, doing this exercise for the first time in late March, wrote three genuinely different alternatives on the whiteboard: Pinaki MedSystems' new patient-engagement module, bundled free into the EMR contracts most hospital chains already held; Prerna CareLine, an outsourced tele-calling service that smaller clinics used to pay nurses or junior staff to phone patients on a schedule; and, for the smallest clinics, literally nothing — a doctor's own memory of which patients seemed worrying at their last visit. Each alternative implied a different buyer, a different budget line, and a different definition of "good."

The second step is to isolate the attributes that are genuinely unique or differentiated relative to each alternative — not attributes that are merely true, but attributes the alternative cannot match at all, or cannot match without becoming a fundamentally different product. Against Pinaki's bundled module, Prakhar's differentiator was a proprietary early-warning algorithm trained on trend data — three consecutive out-of-range readings, not a single bad reading — that Pinaki's module, built as a generic notification feature bolted onto an EMR, could not replicate without years of clinical-data investment. Against Prerna CareLine's human callers, the differentiator was coverage and consistency: an algorithm that watched every patient every day never took a sick day, never had thirty-one accounts to get through before lunch, and never let a quiet, non-complaining patient's numbers drift for three weeks because a louder patient's call ran long.

The third step translates each attribute into the value it delivers to the buyer, in the buyer's own terms — not "trend-based alerting" but "you find the crisis three weeks before it becomes an admission," not "24/7 coverage" but "no patient falls through the cracks because a coordinator was on leave." The fourth step asks, of each value, who actually cares — which is rarely "everyone," and is often not the person in the room. A hospital administrator cared about readmission penalties tied to accreditation scores; a solo clinic owner in Indore cared about staff cost; neither cared, particularly, about the underlying machine-learning architecture that made the alerting possible, though Meera's own engineers found that part the most interesting thing about the product. Only after these four steps — alternatives, differentiated attributes, value, and who cares — does Dunford's method allow a team to name the market category, because the category is simply the shorthand label that best signals, to the specific buyer who cares most, which shelf to mentally place the product on. And a final layer, easy to skip, asks what market trend makes this category matter more this year than it did three years ago — in Meera's case, the fact that Ayushman Bharat empanelment and private insurers alike had begun tying hospital reimbursement more tightly to readmission rates, which made "preventable readmission" a phrase that had real budget behind it in 2024 in a way it had not in 2019.

4. A Worked Example

Consider how the same product priced the same way looks entirely different depending on which frame of reference the buyer applies, and watch the arithmetic rather than take it on faith. Prakhar HealthOS charged clinics ₹149 per enrolled patient per month, all-in. Table 1 lays out what each of the three alternatives Meera's team identified actually cost, and against what basis of comparison — because a positioning choice is, mechanically, a choice about which column a prospect is asked to read first.

Read straight down the "monthly cost per patient" column and the product appears to get steadily more expensive, from free to ₹149. But that is an illusion created by comparing a fixed cost to a variable cost using different units of work — a call, a salary-hour, an outcome — and it is precisely the kind of comparison an unpositioned sales conversation drifts into by accident, because the buyer, not the seller, chooses the frame when no one has chosen it for them. The fourth row does the arithmetic honestly on Prakhar's own terms: if one avoided admission costs the health system roughly ₹40,000, and Prakhar's own product data (drawn from its first forty clinics) showed one admission avoided for every ninety enrolled patients each quarter, then the value delivered per enrolled patient per month works out to ₹40,000 ÷ 90 patients ÷ 3 months ≈ ₹148 — almost exactly Prakhar's own list price. Positioned in that frame, the ₹149 fee is not a cost to be minimized against a coordinator's salary; it is a price set, transparently, at roughly the value it protects, and the sales conversation shifts from "why are you more expensive than an intern" to "here is the arithmetic, and it clears."

Now change one input and watch how much the frame's persuasiveness depends on it. Suppose a skeptical hospital CFO in Pune pushed back on the ninety-patients-per-avoided-admission figure, arguing that Prakhar's early cohort of forty clinics were unusually engaged, hand-picked pilot sites, and that at scale the true rate would be closer to one avoided admission per one hundred and eighty patients — half as effective. Rerun the arithmetic: ₹40,000 ÷ 180 ÷ 3 ≈ ₹74 of value delivered per patient per month against a ₹149 fee, and the frame that looked like a rounding error at ninety patients now shows Prakhar priced at roughly double the value it protects at one hundred and eighty. This is not a hypothetical embarrassment; it is the single most important thing the worked example teaches, because it is exactly the number a sharp buyer will contest, and a positioning statement that cannot survive its own key ratio being halved is not yet a defensible position — it is a slogan waiting to be tested. Meera's team's actual response, when this objection came from a real CFO in April, was to re-run the analysis on Prakhar's full sixty-one-clinic base rather than the original pilot forty, which brought the honest figure to one avoided admission per roughly one hundred and ten patients — value of ₹40,000 ÷ 110 ÷ 3 ≈ ₹121 against the ₹149 fee, a real but narrower margin that they could defend with data rather than optimism, and that became the number sales was trained to use.

5. The Nuances a Learner Must Become Aware Of

Positioning is not messaging, and confusing the two produces confident nonsense

Messaging is the specific words used to communicate a position that has already been chosen — the headline, the deck's third slide, the elevator line. Teams in a hurry frequently skip the analytical work of choosing a frame of reference and jump straight to wordsmithing a tagline, on the theory that a snappier sentence will fix a stalling pipeline. It rarely does, because messaging problems and positioning problems produce the same symptom — prospects who nod politely and never sign — but require opposite fixes. If the frame is wrong, better copy inside that frame only makes the wrong comparison more vivid.

A frame of reference is chosen, not discovered, and the choice can be wrong even when every fact in it is true

Every sentence in Prakhar's readmission-cost framing was factually accurate, yet the frame itself was a judgment call among several equally true options — Meera could instead have framed the product honestly as "workflow software for nurse coordinators," which was also true and would have led to an entirely different, less favorable, comparison against Prerna CareLine's per-call pricing. Positioning work does not ask "what is true about the product," which has many answers, but "which true thing, argued against which honest alternative, gives us the advantage" — a strategic choice, not a discovery exercise, and one a team can get wrong even while writing nothing false.

The buyer's existing mental model outruns your launch deck

A procurement head who has spent three years thinking of Pinaki MedSystems as "the EMR system" will, absent deliberate reframing, slot any new tool into a comparison against Pinaki by default, because that is the shelf already built in his head. Positioning is partly the work of actively dislodging a frame the buyer arrived with, not merely presenting a frame you prefer, and dislodging an existing frame is measurably harder than establishing one in a genuinely blank mind — which is one reason Prakhar's sales cycle with hospital-chain procurement teams, who had strong existing EMR mental models, ran three to four months longer than with independent clinic owners who had none.

Positioning is routinely confused with differentiation, and the two are not the same claim

Differentiation asks what makes a product different; positioning asks, of the differences that exist, which ones matter to a specific buyer comparing against a specific alternative, and how to make that comparison unavoidable. A product can be genuinely, provably different — Prakhar's trend-based alerting algorithm truly was unlike anything in Pinaki's module — and still lose deals, because being different is not the same as being differently valuable to the person holding the budget in the specific moment of comparison the seller has set up.

It cannot manufacture a strength the product does not have

Positioning reframes evaluation; it does not fabricate capability. Had Prakhar's alerting algorithm actually performed no better than a diligent human coordinator checking a spreadsheet twice a day, no frame of reference, however cleverly chosen, would have produced a durable advantage — the readmission-cost frame worked because the underlying product genuinely caught trends two to three weeks earlier than manual review did in Prakhar's own clinical data, a claim the team could and did defend with numbers. A positioning exercise performed on a product with no real edge simply produces an articulate description of mediocrity.

The category label is a consequence, not a lever to be pulled independently

Teams sometimes try to fix a positioning problem by renaming the category — calling the product a "clinical intelligence platform" instead of a "patient-engagement tool" — without changing the underlying alternative, attribute, or value analysis beneath it. A category name chosen before the first four steps are done is decoration; chosen after, it is a genuine compression of real analytical work into two or three words a buyer can file mentally, which is why Dunford's method places it sixth, not first.

Positioning decays as the market moves, even when the product does not change

The trend component of Dunford's method exists because a frame of reference that was persuasive in one year can go stale in the next purely through external change — Prakhar's readmission-cost framing gained force through 2023 and 2024 specifically because insurer reimbursement policy was tightening around readmission rates; had that regulatory trend reversed, the same product, unchanged, would have needed a different frame to stay persuasive, because the thing that made "readmission" a budget-holder's problem would have receded.

A single product can legitimately need more than one position for more than one buyer, and that is not incoherence

Because Prakhar sold into both large hospital chains and small independent clinics, and because those two buyers held genuinely different competitive alternatives in mind — Pinaki's module for one, Prerna CareLine's human callers for the other — Meera's team eventually ran two coherent positioning statements in parallel, one per segment, rather than forcing a single frame to do double duty across buyers who were not actually comparing the product to the same thing.

6. Consumer, B2B and Marketplace — and Early-Stage versus Scale

Positioning's mechanics stay constant across contexts, but the identity of the buyer choosing the frame, and the cost of getting it wrong, shift substantially. In consumer products, the "buyer" and the "frame-chooser" are usually the same distracted individual scrolling a feed for under two seconds before deciding whether to keep reading, which means the competitive-alternatives step must include impulses as legitimate rivals — "doing nothing," "using the free tool already on my phone," "asking a friend" — not just named branded competitors, because those informal alternatives win more often than any competitor's product does. In B2B software like Prakhar's, the frame is chosen collectively and sequentially by several people — a clinic owner, a procurement officer, a hospital's chief medical officer — who may each hold a different alternative in mind, which is exactly the trap Meera fell into before she separated her hospital-chain and independent-clinic positioning; B2B positioning work therefore usually requires mapping frames per buyer role explicitly, not assuming one frame serves the whole buying committee. Marketplace products face a third complication entirely: a marketplace must position twice, once to each side of the transaction, and the two positions can be in tension — a marketplace connecting diabetes coaches to patients, for instance, must position "employment flexibility" to coaches while positioning "verified expertise" to patients, and a frame chosen to flatter one side can actively undercut the other's confidence in the platform.

The difference between an early-stage company and a large one is just as material. An early-stage company, like Prakhar at Series B, typically has almost no brand equity to trade on and must win the frame-of-reference argument fresh in every single sales conversation, which is precisely why Meera's team needed a rehearsed, arithmetic-backed statement rather than a vague aspiration — a small company's positioning has to do real persuasive work because nothing else is carrying it. A large, established company such as Pinaki MedSystems, by contrast, often benefits from a frame the market has already half-accepted on its behalf — "the EMR system everyone already uses" is itself a durable competitive alternative precisely because incumbency has already done the positioning work that a challenger must do explicitly and repeatedly. This is also why repositioning matters more, not less, as a company scales: a position that was sharp at ten customers can calcify into an assumption nobody revisits at six hundred, even as new competitive alternatives (a Pinaki module, a Prerna CareLine expansion) enter and change what "obvious" means.

7. Common Mistakes

The first common mistake is describing features instead of choosing a frame, and its symptom is a sales deck that reads like a specification sheet — a list of things the product does, with no explicit statement of what it should be judged against or instead of. The underlying misunderstanding is treating positioning as a communications problem to be solved with better adjectives, when it is actually a strategic choice about which comparison to force. The cheapest diagnostic is to hand the deck to someone unfamiliar with the product and ask them afterward, cold, "what would you compare this to if you were buying it" — if five different people give five different, unprompted answers, the frame was never chosen, only assumed.

The second common mistake is picking the most flattering frame rather than the most defensible one — a team chooses to compare itself to whichever alternative makes it look best, without checking whether that is the alternative real buyers actually hold in their heads. The symptom is a positioning statement that sales loves reciting internally but that prospects visibly do not recognize in the room, often responding with some version of "that's not really how I was thinking about this." The cheapest diagnostic is simply to ask the last five lost or stalled prospects, directly, what alternative they ultimately chose or seriously considered instead — the honest answer, not the team's preferred answer, is the real frame of reference, and it is often uncomfortable.

The third common mistake is positioning against the whole category rather than the customer's actual alternative, which shows up as messaging that argues broadly against "legacy solutions" or "spreadsheets" in the abstract rather than against the one specific product or workaround a given buyer is actually weighing. This produces technically true but practically weightless claims, because a buyer comparing Prakhar specifically to Prerna CareLine's ₹18-per-call pricing does not care how Prakhar compares to spreadsheets in general. The cheapest diagnostic is to check whether the sales team can name, for the last ten deals, the single specific alternative each prospect was actually evaluating — if the answer is a shrug or a generic category name, the positioning has not actually been tested against reality.

The fourth common mistake, particularly common in fast-scaling companies, is setting a position once at launch and never revisiting it as the competitive set changes — the symptom is a positioning statement that references a competitive alternative that has since become irrelevant, or omits one that has newly become dominant, such as Pinaki's patient-engagement module, which did not exist when Prakhar first launched and only appeared eighteen months later. The cheapest diagnostic is a standing quarterly question, not a one-time workshop: "has anything a buyer would seriously consider instead of us changed in the last ninety days," asked of the sales team directly, because sales hears the answer before product marketing ever does.

8. What Good Looks Like

By early May, Meera's team had run the full exercise twice — once for hospital chains, framed against Pinaki's bundled module and the cost of a preventable readmission, and once for independent clinics, framed against Prerna CareLine and manual coordination, using coordinator time saved rather than admissions avoided as the value metric, since small clinics cared more about freeing a nurse's afternoon than about accreditation scores they were too small to be measured against. Each version named its specific alternative by category, not by brand, in external materials — "the bundled engagement module in your existing EMR" and "outsourced call-based follow-up" — while sales was trained internally to name the actual competitors when a prospect brought them up directly. Each version carried its own arithmetic, rehearsed and defensible under a skeptical CFO's questions, including the honest, lower "per one-hundred-and-ten-patients" figure rather than the flattering pilot-cohort number. Both statements were reviewed quarterly against a standing question about what had changed in the competitive set. The sales team, briefed with two clear frames instead of one blurred one, closed the Nashik hospital-chain deal in July — seventeen weeks after the CFO's initial skepticism, on the arithmetic Meera's team had rebuilt to survive exactly that skepticism — and cut the average enterprise sales cycle from five months to just under three across the following two quarters, because prospects were no longer being asked, implicitly, to compare Prakhar to three different things depending on which conversation they'd had last.

9. What Meera Decided, and What to Learn Next

Meera's decision was not to pick one universal frame of reference for Prakhar HealthOS, but to accept that the company legitimately served two buyers who held two different honest alternatives in their heads, and to build a defensible, arithmetic-backed position for each rather than forcing a single elegant sentence to cover both badly. She resisted, in particular, the temptation to lean on the pilot cohort's flattering ninety-patients-per-admission figure once the full customer base told a more modest and more truthful one hundred and ten — because a position built on a number a smart buyer can falsify in the room is worse than no position at all, and because Series B investors, reading the same data room, needed to see a pipeline built on numbers that would still hold at scale. The reasoning that got her there was Dunford's own ordering: start from what the buyer would actually do without you, not from the category label the company wanted to own, and let the category and the tagline be the last things chosen rather than the first.

From here, the natural next topic to study is how a positioning choice, once made, becomes an actual sentence a sales team can say without notes — the discipline of writing a positioning statement — followed by what happens when a chosen frame of reference is deliberately expanded rather than merely selected, which is the territory of blue ocean strategy and category creation, and by how a chosen frame quietly sets expectations about price before a single number is ever discussed, which is the subject of what pricing signals. Two questions are worth sitting with before moving on. First: for the product you know best, if you asked ten recent customers, unprompted, what they seriously considered instead of you, would their answers converge on one alternative or scatter across several — and if they scatter, whose job is it to have noticed? Second: is there a number in your own current positioning — a cost avoided, a time saved, a risk reduced — that you have tested against your most skeptical customer's most unfavorable honest inputs, or only against your most flattering ones?

Sit with these:
